What began as a bet between friends led him to open over 1,400 cards, ranging from traditional bank-issued to those from airlines, gas stations, and even ice cream shops. Most people have far fewer credit cards. While useful for secure purchasing, handling emergencies, and building credit scores, credit cards can make it difficult to avoid overspending. Globally, the outstanding credit card debt exceeds trillions of dollars. And this is no accident. Credit card companies intentionally design these systems to encourage spending and lock you into a cycle of interest and fees. So, how can you avoid their most common traps? It starts with card selection. Lenders often aggressively advertise perks like cash back, travel miles, and discounts. But these offers only seem generous. In reality, only a small portion of cardholders actually benefit— those who pay off their entire balance every month. But according to one survey, 46% of American cardholders carry a revolving balance. For these users, the cost of interest and fees almost always exceeds the value of rewards. If you think you may fall into this category, financial experts recommend getting a card with the lowest annual percentage rate, or APR. This number is essentially the cost of borrowing money from the credit card company. You pay that cost through interest charges, which kick in as soon as you carry any balance past a statement due date. While APRs are listed as yearly rates, for most cards, interest accrues daily. Currently, we’ve discovered 18 types of hemagglutinin and 11 types of neuraminidase, and different subtypes of influenza A use different combinations. These proteins are necessary for influenza A to enter and exit host cells, so they generally determine which animals a strain can infect. But is it possible for these powerful feelings to endanger your life? In other words, can you actually die from a broken heart? One of the most widely documented medical phenomena addressing this question is the widowhood effect. Studies of elderly couples have found that a person’s risk of dying can increase by up to 90% over the three months following their spouse’s death, leading a significant number of couples to pass away months, weeks, or even days apart. There are a lot of theories explaining this effect. One study found that severe grief and depression were associated with higher levels of inflammatory proteins in the blood, potentially impairing the immune system. And depression, combined with the loss of a supporting partner, can make it hard for a person to keep up with their daily health needs. Similarly, chronic stress can alter hormone levels, impair digestion, and dysregulate the immune system. But while all these factors can reduce life expectancy, there’s another condition where powerful emotions can directly endanger someone’s life: takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Also known as stress cardiomyopathy, or “broken heart syndrome,” this was originally labeled by Japanese doctors in 1990, who named the condition after the Japanese word for an octopus trap. In takotsubo cardiomyopathy, the left ventricle— one of the heart’s four chambers— pools with blood and balloons outward, giving it a distinctively takotsubo-like shape.
